body.p: Passing a PCI device of the host system to the guest gives the guest full control over that device. This is experimental and available on Linux host systems only, see . Consider the following before you use it:

li.p: The guest can change everything the device keeps, such as its firmware and its settings. Treat a device which was in a VM as you treat the guest when you give the device to the host system or to another VM afterwards. To keep the host system from using the device, leave it bound to the vfio-pci driver.

The IOMMU of the host system is what limits the device to the memory of the VM. does not pass a device through without an IOMMU. Do not enable the options of the host kernel which allow passthrough without interrupt remapping.

Devices which the IOMMU cannot tell apart are in one IOMMU group on the host system. They are not protected from each other. Pass a device through only if the other devices in its IOMMU group are not used by the host system or by another VM.
Whoever can open the VFIO device node of a device and the IOMMU device node of the host system controls the device. Give access to them only to the user who runs the VM.

A device which is put into a running VM has to be of the kind the VM was started with before. refuses any other device. Whether a device may be connected to the host system at all, for example the authorization of a Thunderbolt device, is up to the host system.
The state of the device is not part of a saved state or a snapshot of the VM. Saving the state of the VM and taking a snapshot of the running VM are refused while the device is in the VM.
